title: Mechanical Properties of Solids
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Stress-Strain Curve, Hooke's Law, Young's, Bulk & Shear Moduli, Poisson's Ratio & Elastic Potential Energy in Rods
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: Why Do Solids Deform and Spring Back?

When you pull on a rubber band, push a steel spring, or bend a diving board, they distort in shape or size. The moment you let go, they return to their original form. This property of matter by which objects recover their original shape and size after the deforming force is removed is called Elasticity.

Rigid Bodies vs. Elastic Bodies:
In Chapter 06, we assumed rigid bodies never deform. In reality, no body is 100% rigid; all solids deform slightly under heavy loads, and understanding their elastic limits is vital for building bridges, skyscrapers, and aircraft!

topics.title: Stress, Strain, Hooke's Law & The Complete Stress-Strain Curve
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Stress and Strain Definitions
TypeDefinition & FormulaSI Unit & Dimensions
Stress ($\sigma$)Restoring internal force per unit area: $\sigma = \frac{F}{A}$$\text{N/m}^2$ or $\text{Pa}$ ($[M^1 L^{-1} T^{-2}]$)
Strain ($\epsilon$)Fractional change in dimension: $\epsilon = \frac{\Delta l}{l}$Dimensionless ($[M^0 L^0 T^0]$)
1.2 Hooke's Law & The Stress-Strain Curve Regions
$$\text{Hooke's Law:} \quad \boxed{\text{Stress} \propto \text{Strain} \implies \text{Stress} = E \times \text{Strain}}$$

Anatomy of the Stress-Strain Curve (Mild Steel):

  • 1. Proportional Limit (Region $OA$): Stress is directly proportional to strain (Hooke's law holds true).
  • 2. Elastic Limit / Yield Point ($B$): Up to this point, the wire regains its original length completely upon unloading. Beyond $B$, permanent plastic deformation begins.
  • 3. Ultimate Tensile Strength ($D$): The maximum stress the material can withstand before necking and fracture occur at point $E$.
topics.derivationHtml:
Work-Energy Derivation of Elastic Potential Energy in a Stretched Wire

Force required to stretch wire by $x$ is $F = \left(\frac{YA}{L}\right)x$. Work done to stretch by $\Delta l$ is:

$$W = \int_0^{\Delta l} F\,dx = \int_0^{\Delta l} \left(\frac{YA}{L}\right)x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{YA}{L}\right)(\Delta l)^2 = \frac{1}{2}(\text{Stress})(\text{Strain})(\text{Volume})$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Hooke's Law Validity): Hooke's law is not a universal law of nature; it is valid only up to the proportional limit for certain elastic materials.

topics.title: Young's, Bulk & Shear Moduli, Compressibility and Poisson's Ratio
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 The Three Elastic Moduli
Modulus NameDeformation TypeMaster Formula
Young's Modulus ($Y$)Longitudinal (Tensile / Compressive)$Y = \frac{F/A}{\Delta l / l} = \frac{Fl}{A\Delta l}$
Bulk Modulus ($B$)Volumetric (Compressive)$B = -\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta V / V} = -V\frac{dP}{dV}$
Shear Modulus / Rigidity ($\eta$)Shape / Angular Shear$\eta = \frac{F/A}{\theta} = \frac{FL}{A \Delta x}$
2.2 Poisson's Ratio ($\sigma$)
$$\sigma = \frac{\text{Lateral Strain}}{\text{Longitudinal Strain}} = \frac{-\Delta D / D}{\Delta l / l} \qquad (\text{Theoretical limit: } -1.0 \le \sigma \le 0.5)$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Energy Density Stored in Stretched Wire

Energy density $u = \frac{U}{Volume} = \frac{1}{2}(\text{Stress})(\text{Strain}) = \frac{1}{2}Y(\text{Strain})^2 = \frac{\text{Stress}^2}{2Y}$.

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Bulk Modulus Minus Sign): The minus sign in $B = -V(\Delta P/\Delta V)$ is essential because an increase in pressure ($+\Delta P$) always causes a decrease in volume ($-\Delta V$).
